Getting started with WeGrowHealthR

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

WeGrowHealthR takes longitudinal child growth data from raw visits to publication tables and figures. This vignette walks through the first steps that almost every analysis shares: describing your data to the package, cleaning a raw export, computing z-scores and percentiles against the WHO or CDC references, classifying nutritional status, estimating prevalence, drawing growth charts, and tuning any plot. Each section explains the code, the main options, what the output means and where to go next.

All examples use growdat, a simulated school health cohort of about 3,300 children aged 18 months to 18 years with yearly visits. It resembles a large urban school health cohort, so the numbers look like those of the published studies, but they are not findings.

library(WeGrowHealthR)
head(growdat)
#>       pid    sex  site        dob yearvisit   examdate   age height weight
#> 1 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2019 2019-10-25 3.001   95.0   16.0
#> 2 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2020 2020-09-18 3.901  103.1   18.5
#> 3 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2022 2022-12-10 6.127  116.9   23.5
#> 4 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2023 2023-11-29 7.097  122.8   26.1
#> 5 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2024 2024-11-26 8.090  128.6   28.2
#> 6 C000001 Female Site2 2016-10-24      2025 2025-10-24 8.999  134.3   32.5
#>     bmi    haz   waz   baz
#> 1 17.73 -0.015 1.091 1.588
#> 2 17.40  0.252 1.091 1.387
#> 3 17.20  0.202 0.902 1.079
#> 4 17.31  0.262 0.885 0.993
#> 5 17.05  0.260 0.650 0.681
#> 6 18.02  0.296 0.812 0.880

Each row is one visit. pid identifies the child, site the school site, dob and examdate are the date of birth and the date of measurement, and age is the decimal age in years.

1. Describe your data once with wgh_data()

wgh_data() is the data contract. You tell it which of your columns holds each role (child identifier, sex, age or dates, height, weight, site, year) and it returns a wgh_data object with standard column names that every function in the package understands. You do this once per data set.

Ages from dates

If you have the date of birth and the date of measurement, give them as dob and date and leave out age. Age at measurement is computed as the number of days between the two dates divided by 365.25, which is the convention of the WHO software.

gd <- wgh_data(growdat, id = "pid", sex = "sex", dob = "dob", date = "examdate",
               height = "height", weight = "weight", site = "site")
gd
#> <wgh_data>: 8663 visits from 3259 children
#> Ages 1.5 to 18.49 years. Sex: Male 4625, Female 4038
#> Sites: Site1, Site2, Site3
#> Years: 2018 to 2026
#> Mapping: id = pid, sex = sex, dob = dob, date = examdate, height = height,
#> weight = weight, site = site
head(gd$data)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 14
#>   id      sex      age dob        date        year site  height weight   bmi
#>   <chr>   <fct>  <dbl> <date>     <date>     <int> <fct>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 C000001 Female  3.00 2016-10-24 2019-10-25  2019 Site2    95    16    17.7
#> 2 C000001 Female  3.90 2016-10-24 2020-09-18  2020 Site2   103.   18.5  17.4
#> 3 C000001 Female  6.13 2016-10-24 2022-12-10  2022 Site2   117.   23.5  17.2
#> 4 C000001 Female  7.10 2016-10-24 2023-11-29  2023 Site2   123.   26.1  17.3
#> 5 C000001 Female  8.09 2016-10-24 2024-11-26  2024 Site2   129.   28.2  17.1
#> 6 C000001 Female  9.00 2016-10-24 2025-10-24  2025 Site2   134.   32.5  18.0
#> # ℹ 4 more variables: yearvisit <int>, haz <dbl>, waz <dbl>, baz <dbl>

Column names can be given as strings ("pid") or bare names (pid). The printed summary shows the number of children and visits, the age range and the column mapping. year was filled from the date of measurement because no year column was mapped, and BMI was computed from height and weight.

Dates stored as text are read with date_format. Here is a small data set in which dates are written day/month/year, a common format in clinic records:

clinic <- data.frame(
  child = c("A", "A", "B"), gender = c("F", "F", "M"),
  birth = c("03/02/2015", "03/02/2015", "21/11/2012"),
  visit = c("10/09/2021", "12/09/2022", "15/09/2021"),
  ht = c(121.5, 127.0, 134.2), wt = c(23.1, 26.4, 31.0))
wgh_data(clinic, id = "child", sex = "gender", dob = "birth", date = "visit",
         height = "ht", weight = "wt", date_format = "%d/%m/%Y")$data
#> # A tibble: 3 × 9
#>   id    sex      age dob        date        year height weight   bmi
#>   <chr> <fct>  <dbl> <date>     <date>     <int>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 A     Female  6.60 2015-02-03 2021-09-10  2021   122.   23.1  15.6
#> 2 A     Female  7.61 2015-02-03 2022-09-12  2022   127    26.4  16.4
#> 3 B     Male    8.82 2012-11-21 2021-09-15  2021   134.   31    17.2

Sex codes such as "F", "M", 1 and 2, "girl" and "boy" are recognised and stored as "Female" and "Male".

Ages recorded directly

When only age is available, map it with age. The age_unit option takes "years" (default), "months" or "days". When you give both an age column and dates, age_from = "auto" (default) keeps the recorded ages, fills any missing age from the dates, and warns when a recorded age and the date-based age differ by more than 0.1 years. That warning is a useful data quality check. Use age_from = "dates" to always compute age from the dates.

gd2 <- wgh_data(growdat, id = "pid", sex = "sex", age = "age", height = "height",
                weight = "weight", site = "site", year = "yearvisit")
wgh_map(gd2)
#> # A tibble: 7 × 2
#>   role   column   
#>   <chr>  <chr>    
#> 1 id     pid      
#> 2 age    age      
#> 3 sex    sex      
#> 4 height height   
#> 5 weight weight   
#> 6 site   site     
#> 7 year   yearvisit

wgh_map() shows which original column holds each role.

Next steps. Pass gd (or gd$data) to any function. Most functions also accept a plain data frame that already uses the book column names (pid, site, yearvisit), so growdat itself works everywhere.

2. Clean a raw export with wgh_clean()

growdat_raw is the same cohort as a messy export from a school health information system, with heights entered in metres, weights in grams, height and weight swapped, duplicated visits and implausible values.

clean <- wgh_clean(growdat_raw)
attr(clean, "cleaning_log")
#> # A tibble: 11 × 2
#>    step                                                      rows_affected
#>    <chr>                                                             <int>
#>  1 Trimmed spaces in identifiers                                        23
#>  2 Recoded sex values                                                   32
#>  3 Resolved conflicting sex within child                                 0
#>  4 Corrected examination year from the school year                      22
#>  5 Recomputed age from dates                                             0
#>  6 Height in metres converted to cm                                     29
#>  7 Weight in grams converted to kg                                      18
#>  8 Swapped height and weight restored                                   25
#>  9 Duplicate visits removed                                             23
#> 10 Height inconsistent with the child's own series (flagged)            90
#> 11 Rows flagged as implausible                                         104

wgh_clean() repairs only errors whose type is unambiguous and logs every change. Everything else is flagged in the implausible column rather than altered, so you decide what to do with it. The options repair_units, drop_duplicates and z_limit switch individual steps on or off.

Next steps. Inspect the flagged rows with clean[clean$implausible, ], then use the cleaned data in the steps below.

3. Z-scores and percentiles

wgh_add_zscores() adds height-for-age (haz), weight-for-age (waz) and BMI-for-age (baz) z-scores. With reference = "who" (default) it uses the WHO 2006 Child Growth Standards below 60 months and the WHO 2007 Growth Reference from 60 months, with the WHO restricted tails for weight and BMI. The values agree with the anthro and anthroplus packages. With reference = "cdc" it uses the CDC 2000 growth charts (2 to 20 years). percentiles = TRUE adds the matching percentiles.

z_who <- wgh_add_zscores(growdat[1:5, c("pid", "sex", "age", "height", "weight", "bmi")],
                         percentiles = TRUE)
z_who[, c("pid", "age", "haz", "haz_pct", "baz", "baz_pct")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   pid       age     haz haz_pct   baz baz_pct
#>   <chr>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1 C000001  3.00 -0.0157    49.4 1.59     94.4
#> 2 C000001  3.90  0.253     60.0 1.38     91.7
#> 3 C000001  6.13  0.203     58.0 1.08     86.0
#> 4 C000001  7.10  0.261     60.3 0.993    84.0
#> 5 C000001  8.09  0.261     60.3 0.681    75.2
z_cdc <- wgh_add_zscores(growdat[1:5, c("pid", "sex", "age", "height", "weight", "bmi")],
                         reference = "cdc")
z_cdc[, c("pid", "age", "haz", "baz")]
#> # A tibble: 5 × 4
#>   pid       age    haz   baz
#>   <chr>   <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 C000001  3.00 0.270  1.35 
#> 2 C000001  3.90 0.693  1.35 
#> 3 C000001  6.13 0.248  1.06 
#> 4 C000001  7.10 0.122  0.904
#> 5 C000001  8.09 0.0850 0.566

The two references differ, most for BMI, because they were built from different populations and periods. Weight-for-age is not defined by WHO after 10 years or by CDC before 2 years, so those cells are missing.

For single values, wgh_zscore() takes the measurement, age, sex and indicator. wgh_compare_references() shows several versions side by side, which helps when you need to explain why two software packages disagree:

wgh_zscore(130, age = 9, sex = "Female", indicator = "hfa")
#> [1] -0.4082059
wgh_zscore(130, age = 9, sex = "Female", indicator = "hfa", reference = "cdc")
#> [1] -0.4738933
wgh_compare_references(c(22, 28), age = c(10, 15), sex = "Male", indicator = "bfa")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>     age sex   value   who who_plain_lms symmetric   cdc anthroplus
#>   <dbl> <chr> <dbl> <dbl>         <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl>      <dbl>
#> 1    10 Male     22  2.16          2.16      2.73  1.63       2.16
#> 2    15 Male     28  2.18          2.18      2.83  1.81       2.18

The columns are the WHO value with restricted tails (who), the plain LMS value without them (who_plain_lms), a symmetric approximation, the CDC value, and the anthroplus value when that package is installed.

You can also give your own reference as a data frame with columns sex, age (years), L, M and S (and optionally indicator), for example a national growth reference.

4. Nutritional status with wgh_classify()

wgh_classify() adds z-scores and status categories. The WHO system (default) uses BMI-for-age cut-offs of -3 and -2 SD for severe thinness and thinness, +1 and +2 SD for overweight and obesity from 5 years (+2 and +3 SD below 5 years), and HAZ below -2 (and -3) for stunting (and severe stunting). The CDC system uses the 5th, 85th and 95th BMI percentiles.

cl <- wgh_classify(growdat)
table(cl$bmi_status[cl$age >= 5], cl$sex[cl$age >= 5])
#>                  
#>                   Male Female
#>   Severe thinness   18     11
#>   Thinness          71     59
#>   Normal          1825   2178
#>   Overweight       872    622
#>   Obesity          762    200
cl_cdc <- wgh_classify(growdat[growdat$age >= 2, ], system = "cdc")
table(cl_cdc$bmi_status, cl_cdc$sex)
#>                 
#>                  Male Female
#>   Underweight     397    300
#>   Healthy weight 2478   2811
#>   Overweight      765    540
#>   Obesity         826    240

Besides the categories, the output has indicator columns such as overweight_obesity, obesity, stunting and thinness (TRUE or FALSE), ready for prevalence estimation.

5. Prevalence and trends

wgh_prevalence() estimates the prevalence of an indicator, or the share of each category of a status variable, with confidence intervals. by sets the groups. For a categorical status, method = "sison_glaz" gives simultaneous intervals for all categories together, as in Ho et al. (2026, Sci Rep 16:7515).

older <- cl[cl$age >= 5, ]
wgh_prevalence(older, "bmi_status", by = "sex", method = "sison_glaz")
#> # A tibble: 10 × 7
#>    sex    category            n cases prevalence  lower upper
#>    <chr>  <chr>           <int> <int>      <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
#>  1 Male   Severe thinness  3548    18      0.507  0      2.26
#>  2 Male   Thinness         3548    71      2.00   0.254  3.76
#>  3 Male   Normal           3548  1825     51.4   49.7   53.2 
#>  4 Male   Overweight       3548   872     24.6   22.8   26.3 
#>  5 Male   Obesity          3548   762     21.5   19.7   23.2 
#>  6 Female Severe thinness  3070    11      0.358  0      1.98
#>  7 Female Thinness         3070    59      1.92   0.326  3.54
#>  8 Female Normal           3070  2178     70.9   69.3   72.6 
#>  9 Female Overweight       3070   622     20.3   18.7   21.9 
#> 10 Female Obesity          3070   200      6.51   4.92   8.14
pv <- wgh_prevalence(older, "overweight_obesity", by = c("sex", "yearvisit"))
head(pv)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 7
#>   sex    yearvisit     n cases prevalence lower upper
#>   <chr>      <int> <int> <int>      <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Male        2018   163    79       48.5  40.9  56.1
#> 2 Female      2018   127    35       27.6  20.5  35.9
#> 3 Male        2019   485   250       51.5  47.1  56.0
#> 4 Female      2019   429   127       29.6  25.5  34.1
#> 5 Male        2020   516   259       50.2  45.9  54.5
#> 6 Female      2020   444   139       31.3  27.2  35.8

Each row gives the number of visits (n), the number with the condition (cases), the prevalence in percent and its interval. A trend over calendar time is tested with the Cochran-Armitage test:

wgh_trend_test(older, "overweight_obesity", "yearvisit", by = "sex")
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   sex    test             statistic    df   p_value first  last
#>   <chr>  <chr>                <dbl> <dbl>     <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1 Male   Cochran-Armitage      19.3     1 0.0000110  48.5  40.5
#> 2 Female Cochran-Armitage      12.8     1 0.000348   27.6  21.8

A small p-value says the prevalence changes steadily across years. Repeated visits of the same child are not independent, so for formal inference on trends use the GEE models in wgh_gee_trend(), which the trend flows apply (see vignette("trends-malnutrition")).

wgh_plot_prevalence(pv)

6. Growth charts

wgh_plot_growth_chart() draws a child’s measurements over reference curves. Two choices matter:

  • lines = "percentile" (default) draws percentile curves, set with centiles (default 3, 15, 50, 85 and 97). lines = "sd" draws z-score curves, set with sd_lines (default -3 to +3).
  • reference = "who" (default), "cdc" or your own LMS table.

indicator chooses height ("hfa"), weight ("wfa") or BMI ("bfa"), and age_range the ages shown.

girl <- growdat$pid[growdat$sex == "Female"][1]
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl)

wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl, lines = "sd")

wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = girl, indicator = "bfa", reference = "cdc",
                      centiles = c(5, 50, 85, 95), band = TRUE)

The CDC BMI chart marks the 85th and 95th percentiles, the CDC cut-offs for overweight and obesity. Several children can be shown together, each in its own colour, with child_colour = NULL:

three <- unique(growdat$pid[growdat$sex == "Female"])[1:3]
wgh_plot_growth_chart(growdat, ids = three, child_colour = NULL, age_range = c(2, 14))

Next steps. To judge whether a child’s growth follows the expected course given the child’s own history, rather than the population, use the conditional references in vignette("growth-distributions").

7. Tuning any plot

Every plot function and plot() method in the package accepts the same display options through .... They are documented in ?wgh_plot_options: titles and axis labels, base_size, legend position, a palette, point_size, line_width, alpha, show_ci, facets and axis limits.

wgh_plot_prevalence(pv, title = "Overweight or obesity, 5 to 18 years",
                    palette = c(Male = "black", Female = "grey55"),
                    show_ci = FALSE, y_limits = c(0, 50), base_size = 12, legend = "right")
#> Warning: No shared levels found between `names(values)` of the manual scale and the
#> data's fill values.

To use the same settings for several plots, build them once:

opts <- wgh_plot_options(base_size = 9, legend = "none")
do.call(wgh_plot_prevalence, c(list(pv), opts))

Plots are ggplot objects, so you can also add any ggplot2 layer, scale or theme, and save them with wgh_save_figure() (TIFF and PDF at 600 dpi by default, the format most journals ask for).

8. Tracking the analytic sample

Analyses usually restrict the data step by step. wgh_sample_flow() records how many children and visits remain after each step and, when there is a site column, the share retained at each site. A step that removes one site much more than the others is flagged, because it can bias comparisons.

fl <- wgh_sample_flow(growdat,
  "Ages 5 to 18" = ~ age >= 5 & age <= 18.5,
  "At least 3 visits" = wgh_min_visits(3))
fl
#> <wgh_sample_flow>: 2 restriction steps
#> # A tibble: 3 × 5
#>   step              children visits children_lost pct_children_retained
#>   <chr>                <int>  <int>         <int>                 <dbl>
#> 1 Start                 3259   8663            NA                 100  
#> 2 Ages 5 to 18          2580   6618           679                  79.2
#> 3 At least 3 visits     1099   4570          1481                  33.7
#> Children retained by site (%):
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   step              `% Site1` `% Site2` `% Site3`
#>   <chr>                 <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 Start                 100       100       100  
#> 2 Ages 5 to 18           79.2      79.9      77.2
#> 3 At least 3 visits      34.1      34        30.8
plot(fl)

The restricted data are in fl$data.

9. Run modes, reports and export

Heavy functions read their defaults (bootstrap replicates, folds, quantile grids, subsample sizes) from a run mode. wgh_config("dev") gives settings that run in seconds for checking code, "analysis" is the default and "publication" uses full grids and bootstraps. Any argument you pass explicitly overrides the mode, and single settings can be overridden with wgh_config("analysis", B = 1000).

old <- wgh_config("dev")
#> WeGrowHealthR run mode: dev
wgh_opt("B")
#> [1] 10

The study workflows (wgh_flow_*()) return a wgh_report that holds every table, figure and model of one study, the analytic sample flow and the status of each model (fitted, failed or skipped, with the reason).

rep <- wgh_flow_malnutrition_trends(growdat, mode = "dev")
rep
#> 
#> ── Stunting, thinness, obesity and double burden (Ho et al. 2026, medRxiv 2026.07.26.26358982) ──
#> 
#> Tables (6): table1, prevalence_by_year, trend_tests, gee_odds_ratios,
#> double_burden, median_by_site
#> Figures (4): fig_trends, fig_status_bars, fig_dbm_heatmap, fig_or_forest
#> Model status: 4 ok, 0 failed, 0 skipped
#> ok: GEE calendar trend, stunting (warning: Skipping age group(s) 10-14 y, 15-18
#> y with fewer than 10 events. | Skipping age group(s) 5-9 y, 10-14 y with fewer
#> than 10 events.)
#> ok: GEE calendar trend, obesity (warning: Skipping age group(s) <5 y with fewer
#> than 10 events.)
#> Settings: mode = dev; n_children = 3259
rep$tables$prevalence_by_year        # a table
plot(rep, "fig_trends", base_size = 13)       # a figure, restyled
wgh_export(rep, "malnutrition_results")       # Excel workbook, TIFF and PDF figures

Where to go next

  • vignette("trends-malnutrition"): secular trends, prevalence, the double burden of malnutrition and GEE trend models.
  • vignette("trajectories"): how a prepubertal exposure relates to later height trajectories with mixed models.
  • vignette("growth-curves"): SITAR growth curves, the pubertal spurt, its timing, intensity and duration.
  • vignette("growth-distributions"): quantile regression, growth inequality and conditional growth references.
  • vignette("phenotypes-states"): growth phenotypes, canalization and multistate models.
  • vignette("prediction"): predicting late-adolescent height and explaining predictions.
  • vignette("simulated-data") and vignette("reproducing-the-program"), which runs all 14 study flows.
  • vignette("parallel-computing"): running bootstraps, quantile grids and cross-validation on several cores with identical results.

wgh_references() lists the studies whose analyses the package reproduces.
